data.title: Default Credentials on Administrative Web Interface
data.summary:
Administrative web interfaces were accessible using vendor default credentials,
granting full control of the affected applications and, in several cases, command
execution on the underlying host.
data.description:
Applications exposing web-based management interfaces retained the
credentials assigned by the vendor at installation. These values are published in
product documentation and are held in publicly available wordlists, so no
guessing is required.

Administrative access to this type of application often extends beyond
the application itself. Build and automation platforms provide script execution
by design; application servers permit the deployment of arbitrary archives;
monitoring systems allow the definition of commands executed on managed hosts.
In each case, administrator access gives command
execution on the server.

Authentication performed with valid credentials produces no failed login events
and appears legitimate in application logs, so the activity is unlikely to be
detected by controls that monitor for authentication failures.

Successful authentication using default credentials was confirmed during testing.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to these interfaces could obtain full
administrative control of the affected applications without any prior credential
material. Where the application provides script or command execution
functionality, this results in code execution on the underlying operating system
and a foothold within the internal network, from which the wider environment can
be attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Change all default credentials immediately to values meeting the
   organisation's password standard, and review the affected applications for
   evidence of prior unauthorised access.

2. Where the application permits it, rename or disable the built-in
   administrative account rather than only changing its password.

3. Enable multi-factor authentication on all administrative interfaces where the
   application supports it.

4. Restrict network access to management interfaces so that they are reachable
   only from dedicated administrative networks, using host and network firewall
   rules rather than relying on the application's own access control.

5. Introduce a build review step that verifies default credentials have been
   changed and unnecessary management interfaces disabled before any system is
   placed into production.

6. Maintain an inventory of applications exposing management interfaces and audit
   it periodically, as such interfaces are frequently enabled by default and
   forgotten.
